Meeting Date:  October 1, 2026
From:  Genoveva Rocha, City Clerk
Department:  City Clerk
Submitted by:  Sandra Dolson, Deputy City Clerk

Subject
Selection of Chair and Vice Chair

Recommendation
Select one member to serve as Chairperson and one member to serve as Vice Chairperson for
the term ending on June 30, 2027.

Background
The Business and Industry Commission (Commission) consists of seven members, including
three Business Representatives, one Council Member, one individual employed by a business
in Vernon or a Labor Representative, and two Real Estate Representatives. Members serve a
term of four years and may be reappointed. Members serve no more than two consecutive full
four-year terms.

Pursuant to Vernon Municipal Code (VMC) Section 2.52.100.B., members are required to elect
a Chairperson and Vice Chairperson annually from different appointing categories under Section
2.52.050. Additionally, a member may not serve as Chairperson for more than two consecutive
terms. The VMC is silent on term limits for the Vice Chairperson.

The Commission appointed former Commission Members Thomas Condon to serve as
Chairperson and Hector Morfin to serve as Vice Chairperson on October 2, 2025; however, their
terms on the Commission ended on June 30, 2026. To fill open positions, the Vernon City Council
appointed new members to the Commission on June 16, 2026. The following are the current
members:

Commissioner  Appointing Category  Date Appointed  End of Term
Brian Bailey  Business Representative  June 4, 2024  June 30, 2028
Catherine Browne  Business Representative  June 16, 2026  June 30, 2030
Ronit Edry  Business Representative  June 16, 2026  June 30, 2030
Melissa Ybarra  Council Member  June 4, 2024  June 30, 2028
Jacquie Cabrera  Employee/Labor Representative  June 16, 2026  June 30, 2030
Paul Sablock  Real Estate Representative  June 4, 2024  June 30, 2028
Miles Solomon  Real Estate Representative  June 16, 2026  June 30, 2030

All members of the Commission are eligible to serve as Chairperson and Vice Chairperson. The
Commission should select a Chairperson and Vice Chairperson to serve through June 30, 2027.

3.  Vernon Public Utilities Electric Cost of Service and Rate Design Study Update
  Recommendation: Receive and file a presentation and provide feedback on the
  Electric Cost of Service and Rate Design Study.

  Public Utilities General Manager Dusenberry presented the staff report, and Assistant
  General Manager Richard Corbi conducted a PowerPoint presentation.

  Commission members asked clarifying questions about the data presented by staff,
  specifically the Energy Cost Adjustment (ECA) and Renewable Portfolio Standards
  (RPS). They opined that the two rates should remain separate on the billing statements.

  City Administrator Saeki provided information on the ECA and RPS rates and noted
  that information on the matter would be brought back and ready before the next budget.
  He acknowledged the Commission recommendation to keep these two rates separate.

  Chairperson Condon invited public comments.

  Marisa Olguin, Vernon Chamber of Commerce, requested the Commission to make an
  official recommendation after hearing all the policies. She noted that she found the
  discussion and presentations to be transparent.

  Steve Kim, Financial Pacific American Fish Company, noted that he initially thought the
  8% increase was unreasonable given rising costs of raw materials, packaging, labor,
  and fuel. However, he appreciated the City’s willingness to find a reasonable solution.

  Commissioner Ybarra moved and Vice Chairperson Morfin seconded a motion to
  receive and file a presentation on the Electric Cost of Service and Rate Design Study
  with a recommendation to the City Council to increase the electric rate to 4% for one
  year and to keep the ECA and RPS separate on the billing statements. The question
  was called and the motion carried 6-1, Commissioner Browne voting in opposition.

2.  Fiscal Year 2026-27 Proposed Budget Overview
  Recommendation: Receive and file a presentation and provide feedback on the
  Proposed Budget for Fiscal Year 2026-27.

  City Administrator Saeki presented the staff report.

  Chairperson Condon called for a recess at 10:41 a.m.

  Commissioner Ybarra left the meeting at 10:41 a.m.

  Chairperson Condon reconvened the regular meeting at 10:47 a.m.

  Finance Director Hui presented the current budget and the proposed budget for FY
  2026-27.

  Commissioner Bailey expressed concern that safety costs were half of the budget.
  Finance Director Hui responded that it included the pension liability, which was on top
  of the contract with the Los Angeles County Fire Department. City Administrator Saeki
  also noted that it included workers’ compensation, and the amount was in line with
  contract cities.

  The board briefly discussed workers' compensation, liabilities, settlements, the
  provisions and contract costs associated with the Los Angeles County Fire Department,
  and the need to hire for the police department to compensate for future retirements.

  Commissioner Browne commented that the General Fund showed revenue from the
  Utility Users Tax (UUT), which accounted for 17% of the budget. She pointed out that
  utility users are currently paying a 6% temporary UUT, in addition to the ECS/RPS/PCA
  (Power Cost Adjustments) charges, not including the proposed 8% rate increase. City
  Administrator Saeki mentioned that staff would present additional information for the
  Commission's discussion and consideration regarding the long-term rate increase that
  the Vernon City Council should evaluate.

  Chairperson Condon commented that the increases seemed significantly high and that
  a special parcel tax was difficult for brokers when trying to sell Vernon as a business-
  friendly city. He stated that the parcel tax is not found in neighboring jurisdictions,
  prospective business owners do not have a clear understanding of the tax, and

  City Administrator Saeki said staff would take the Commission's comments and

ORAL REPORTS
4.  Brief Reports, Announcements, or Directives to Staff
  City Administrator Saeki announced a study session the following week to discuss the
  citywide budget and a “Business Breakfast” to share information presented to the
  Commission. He shared that the City was working with the Cities of Commerce,
  Industry, and Santa Fe Springs, which have formed a coalition called the Big 4 to
  advocate at the state and federal levels for industrial cities and secure funding for
  different uses. He shared that the California State Senate passed a significant piece of
  legislation, Senate Bill 1274, and the Big 4 would continue working with lobbyists to
  have it move through the House.

  He provided an update on the Link US. lawsuit, noting that staff would meet with BNSF
  Railway, as they have in the past. Regarding the California High Speed Rail project, he
  said the City was continuing to oppose it because of the impact it would have on
  businesses near 26th Street.

  Commissioner Sachdeva announced that he had completed his term on the
  Commission and that this would be his last meeting as a member. He expressed
  appreciation for his time served and encouraged City stakeholders and the City of
  Vernon governing bodies to continue advocating for businesses and property owners
  in the City.

   Business and Industry Commission Agenda Report

Meeting Date:  October 1, 2026
From:  Brian Saeki, City Administrator
Department:  City Administration
Submitted by:  Lilia Hernandez, Deputy City Administrator

Subject
Business Tax Contribution Study

Recommendation
A. Receive and file a presentation on the findings of the Business Tax Contribution Study; and
B. Provide feedback and/or recommendation(s) regarding potential changes to the City’s
Warehouse Special Parcel Tax, Public Safety Special Parcel Tax, and Utility Users Tax.

Background
The City’s Utility Users Tax (UUT) generates approximately $14 million each year, which
represents more than 15% of the City’s total revenues, making it the City’s second largest
revenue source. The UUT (Measure R) was passed by voters in 2018 and is scheduled to sunset
in 2028. In anticipation of the expiration of the UUT, on October 21, 2025, the City Council
received a presentation on the potential of placing a measure on the April 2026 ballot to extend
the UUT. Subsequently, a presentation was also made to the Business and Industry Commission
(BIC) and discussed at a Business Breakfast in late 2025. The business community expressed
concerns regarding the parity, or lack thereof, in the tax contributions paid by different business
sectors within the City, and it was suggested that the City undertake a study to evaluate whether
different business types contribute their fair share in taxes for their use of City infrastructure and
services.

Subsequently, the City engaged Kosmont & Associates, Inc. (Kosmont) to conduct a business
tax contribution study. Kosmont conducted an analysis of municipal fees and taxes paid by the
various types of businesses located in the City including Business License Tax, Public Safety
Parcel Tax, Sales Tax, Utility Users Tax, etc., to determine whether adjustments were necessary
to ensure parity. The goal for the study was to identify any disparity and determine whether there
is a need to restructure the various taxes to balance out the overall tax burden carried by various
industries and/or categories of business operations in the City.

The results of Kosmont’s analysis identified disparities in the tax contributions paid by different
business types. The study concluded that the per square footage tax contribution of cold storage
and higher value manufacturing facilities (large utility users) was nearly double that of the per
square footage tax contributions paid by warehouse and hybrid/lower value manufacturing type
businesses. The results further indicated that many high value manufacturers may be facing
significant tax burdens unrelated to local City service impacts and that a reduction in UUT for
high utility usage businesses may be warranted. Given the study results, staff developed potential
options for restructuring the Warehouse Special Parcel Tax, Public Safety Special Parcel Tax,
and Utility Users Tax to achieve greater parity among different business types while maintaining
approximately the same overall level of City tax revenue.

The study results and options for restructuring these taxes were shared at a recent Business
Breakfast on September 10, 2026. The study results and options will be presented to the BIC at
its Special Meeting on October 1, 2026 to gather input and feedback to be shared with the City
Council. The goal of extending and/or restructuring certain taxes is not to increase revenue, but

  Item 3  Page 10 of 14
 rather maintain approximately the same level of revenue while addressing identified disparities
in the distribution of tax burden among different business sectors.

Next steps
Staff will share feedback and any recommendations received from the BIC with City Council
when the study results are presented. City Council will then consider the information and
determine whether to place any tax measures on the ballot for the April 2027 Municipal General
Election.

Strategic Plan Goals
Goal 2: Promote Economic Growth and Revenue Generation

Fiscal Impact
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report.

Meeting Date:  October 1, 2026
From:  Daniel S. Wall, P.E., Director of Public Works-City Engineer
Department:  Public Works
Submitted by:  Daniel S. Wall, P.E., Director of Public Works-City Engineer

Subject
Potential New Regulation of Data Centers and Cold Storage Warehouse Development

Recommendation
Consider the information presented and provide input and recommendations on whether and
in what manner to adopt regulations governing data center and cold storage warehouse uses
in the I Zone.

Background
Since at least 2007, data centers and cold storage warehouses have been permitted uses
under Vernon Municipal Code (VMC) Section 17.22.020. “Permitted uses” are land uses
allowed as a matter of right within the industrial zone of the City and do not require any
separate City Council or discretionary approval. For permitted or by-right uses, the project
approval process is ministerial and the City’s review is administrative, designed to ensure that
the proposed development adheres to existing general plan and zoning rules and meets
existing legal standards for building quality, health, and safety.

There is currently one operating data center in the City of Vernon and several other data center
projects at varying stages in the development process. The City Council has recognized that
data center projects have generated many questions within the community and directed staff
to analyze and provide recommendations regarding changing the use from permitted/by-right
to a regulatory framework designed to ensure City Council discretion and public engagement
through a transparent process that addresses community and environmental impacts.

City Council also directed staff to analyze changing cold storage warehouse uses from
permitted/by-right to a regulatory process with additional oversight in response to community
health and safety concerns in the aftermath of the Lineage fire in Boyle Heights.

The Vernon Business and Industry Commission (BIC) was created to assist with making the
City of Vernon more attractive to employees, businesses, and investors, while appropriately
considering the needs and concerns of the residential communities within and in close
proximity to the City. Accordingly, staff are bringing this item to the BIC in advance of City
Council's consideration in order to obtain the Commission's input and recommendations on
the appropriate regulatory approach, given the Commission's role representing the
perspective of Vernon's business and industrial community. Any proposed changes would
need to be made via an Ordinance of the City Council.

Regulatory Options
In evaluating regulatory options, staff focused on the Conditional Use Permit (CUP) and
Development Agreement (DA) processes.

A CUP is a discretionary entitlement that allows a use not permitted by right, subject to specific
findings such as consistency with the General Plan, compatibility with surrounding uses,
adequate infrastructure, and a determination that the use is not detrimental to public health

  Item 4  Page 12 of 14
 and safety. If the necessary findings can be made, the CUP generally must be approved. The
City may attach conditions reasonably related to mitigating the impacts of the specific use,
such as traffic, noise, hours of operation, screening, and odor control. These conditions must
be connected to and proportionate to the project's impacts. Any fee associated with a CUP is
likewise subject to nexus and proportionality requirements; a generic community benefit fee
not linked to a specific impact would be vulnerable to legal challenge.

A DA is a contract between the City and a property owner that allows negotiation of financial
terms and conditions, such as contributions to community benefits and other broader
advantages. Unlike a CUP, these benefits are not strictly linked to the project's direct impacts.

A CUP and a DA serve distinct legal functions, and relying on a DA alone may surrender key
regulatory authority preserved by a CUP:

  •  Contract versus permit: A DA is a bilateral contract authorized under Government
  Code Section 65864 et seq. Its statutory purpose is to provide developer certainty by
  vesting the rules in place at approval. Conversely, a CUP is a discretionary land use
  permit issued under the City’s police power, allowing the City to retain ongoing
  regulatory oversight rather than being bound strictly by contract terms.

  •  Legal nexus and financial scope: CUP conditions and fees must satisfy strict legal
  nexus and proportionality requirements tied directly to project impacts (e.g., traffic,
  noise, screening). A generic "community benefit fee" imposed through a CUP would be
  vulnerable to legal challenge. In contrast, a DA allows the City to negotiate broader
  financial contributions and community benefits that are not strictly limited to direct
  impact mitigation

  •  Enforcement mechanism: Violating a CUP condition is a code enforcement issue that
  the City can resolve administratively, including permit modification or revocation
  through a public hearing. Violating a DA constitutes a contract breach, requiring court
  litigation—a process that is slower, costlier, and may not automatically halt ongoing site
  operations during the dispute.

  •  Periodic review and unilateral updates: The City can condition a CUP to require
  periodic operational reviews, giving staff the authority to adjust or strengthen conditions
  over time. A DA cannot be modified unilaterally by the City; any amendment requires
  the developer's mutual consent.

  •  CEQA mitigation enforcement: While both entitlements trigger project-level CEQA
  review and mitigation requirements, their enforcement tools differ significantly.
  Mitigation measures imposed via a CUP are enforced administratively, whereas DA
  mitigation measures must be enforced through court action.

Because a CUP and a DA serve different legal purposes and offer different enforcement tools,
the Commission may wish to consider both the certainty a DA offers developers and the ongoing
regulatory flexibility a CUP preserves for the City in formulating its recommendation.

Any proposed new regulations would apply to projects and developments not yet permitted or
approved as of the effective date of the ordinance. The City cannot unilaterally impose new or
additional regulations on existing projects where there are approved permits, a contractual
relationship, and substantial investment by the developer, without risking legal action.

  Item 4  Page 13 of 14
 Options for consideration include the following:

  1. Requiring a CUP for new data center and cold storage warehouse uses in the I Zone.
  2. Requiring both a CUP and DA, while providing City Council authority, in its sole
  discretion, the ability to waive the DA requirement on a case-by-case basis upon
  specified findings.
  3. Requiring a CUP (with or without DA) for new data center uses only. Cold storage
  warehouses make up an important segment of the City’s business community and
  economy and serve an essential function in the region; staff have had limited time to
  study the potential impacts of additional regulatory requirements for cold storage uses.
  If the direction is to prioritize data center regulation, staff can focus the ordinance on
  those changes and come back at a later time with further analysis and
  recommendations regarding cold storage regulation.
  4. Leave the Municipal Code unchanged and continue to seek feedback. Under this
  approach, data centers and cold storage warehouses would remain permitted/by-right
  uses unless and until City Council takes further action.

Next Steps
Staff will present their analysis as well as the BIC’s input and recommendations to City Council
at an upcoming meeting, likely in late October. If City Council directs staff to prepare an ordinance
incorporating some or all of the proposed regulations, the ordinance will be duly noticed for a
public hearing and considered by City Council for first reading not less than 20 days after the
hearing notice is published. If approved, the ordinance and new regulations would take effect 30
days after second reading and adoption by City Council.
Strategic Plan Goals
Goal 3: Advance Sustainability and Environmental Stewardship

There is no fiscal impact associated with this report.
